strengths: The paper identifies a real and underexplored issue in FS-PCS: FPS-based prototype construction is unstable and sensitive to initialization. Table 1 provides direct empirical evidence, and the motivation is well argued.

The proposed WARM module is simple, architecture-agnostic, and easy to integrate. The whitening-cross-attention-coloring design is technically plausible, and the ablation in Table 5 supports the necessity of both whitening and coloring.

The empirical results are strong and consistent across two benchmarks (S3DIS and ScanNet) and multiple settings (1/2-way, 1/5-shot). For example, on S3DIS the method improves overall mIoU from 51.03 (FPS+min-dist) to 55.66 and substantially outperforms COSeg (43.64).

The paper provides useful auxiliary analyses: attention entropy/diversity (Table 6), qualitative attention maps (Fig. 4), gradient magnitude and validation convergence (Fig. 5), and prototype token count sensitivity (Fig. 6). These help explain why the method works.
The writing is generally clear, with a well-organized method section, informative figures, and a transparent description of the main components.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: the individual components (ZCA whitening, cross-attention, inverse coloring) are known, and the combination, while effective, is relatively straightforward. The paper does not discuss related whitening-based few-shot segmentation or style-transfer WCT approaches, which would help position the contribution.

The method is described primarily for 1-way 1-shot, but the experiments include 2-way settings. The paper does not explain how WARM handles multiple foreground classes: whether separate prototypes/tokens are learned per class, how the margin loss is extended to multi-class, and how the FG/BG formulation generalizes. This is a significant clarity and reproducibility gap.

Important implementation details for whitening are missing: covariance inversion may be singular or unstable with few support points and high-dimensional features. The paper does not specify regularization, pseudo-inverse, epsilon, or the minimum number of points required, making exact reproduction difficult.

The experimental evaluation is limited to two indoor datasets (S3DIS, ScanNet) and lacks outdoor LiDAR or cross-dataset transfer. Several recent FS-PCS baselines are not compared, and main results report only mean mIoU without variance/confidence intervals or statistical significance tests.

The training objective includes a simplification loss (Eq. 15) with hyperparameter lambda, but there is no ablation on its contribution or sensitivity. Runtime and memory costs of the per-episode covariance computation and inverse square root are not reported.
The title/abstract use 'White Aggregation' rather than 'Whitening Aggregation', which is confusing given the method relies on whitening. Minor but worth correcting.

strengths: Identifies and convincingly quantifies an under-explored problem: the instability of FPS-based prototype construction in FS-PCS, supported by a distributional analysis over 1000 FPS initializations (Table 1) showing large performance swings, and by the observation that a naive min-distance baseline can rival more complex pipelines.

The proposed WARM module is simple, principled, and well-motivated: sandwiching cross-attention between ZCA whitening and its inverse coloring is an interpretable way to close the distributional gap between prototypical tokens and support features, and the mechanism is clearly explained (Sec. 4.2, Sec. 5).

Strong and largely consistent empirical gains: state-of-the-art overall mIoU on S3DIS (55.66 vs. 51.03) and ScanNet (41.21 vs. 39.01), with best results across most of the 1/2-way and 1/5-shot settings.

Thorough and insightful analysis: the component ablation (Table 5) makes the non-obvious point that whitening alone degrades performance while whitening+coloring recovers and surpasses it; attention entropy/diversity (Table 6), token-count sensitivity (Fig. 6), and gradient-magnitude/convergence analyses (Fig. 5) collectively support the alignment hypothesis.
Clear presentation with effective qualitative evidence (Fig. 1, 3, 4) that directly illustrates the misalignment problem and the resulting segmentation improvements.
Reproducibility is aided by concrete implementation details (datasets, splits, optimizer, learning rate schedule, hardware, token counts) and an ablation over the number of prototypical tokens.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: whitening/coloring (ZCA decorrelation) is a long-established technique (e.g., decorrelated batch normalization), so the core contribution is its application and analysis in the FS-PCS prototype-generation context rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. This is a 'simple yet effective' contribution whose value rests heavily on the empirical results.

The blanket 'state-of-the-art with a significant margin' claim is not uniformly true: on ScanNet 1-way 1-shot, COSeg outperforms WARM (41.78 vs. 40.13, bolded as best in Table 4). This inconsistency is not acknowledged or discussed, and it slightly weakens the generality of the claim.

Prototype construction is framed around a foreground/background split; how the whitening/cross-attention behaves for general N-way multi-class episodes (many classes, per-class covariance estimation) is not fully discussed, leaving scalability questions open.

No computational or runtime analysis is provided, even though whitening requires estimating and inverting a DxD covariance matrix (Eqs. 8-9); numerical stability (ill-conditioned covariance) and cost relative to FPS baselines are not addressed.
All experiments use a single frozen backbone (Stratified Transformer), so the generality of the whitening-alignment benefit across other feature extractors is untested.
Evaluation reports mean mIoU over episodes without any statistical significance testing or confidence intervals, making it hard to judge whether some of the smaller margins are meaningful.

strengths: Targets a genuinely under-explored aspect of FS-PCS: prototype construction rather than query-side adaptation. The empirical demonstration that FPS-based prototypes are unstable (Tab. 1, std 2.41 mIoU for COSeg across 1000 FPS initializations) is a useful, quantified observation for the community.

The proposed WARM module is simple, practical and easy to bolt onto an existing frozen backbone: whitening -> cross-attention -> coloring. The idea of matching the distributions of learnable prototypical tokens and support features before attention is sensible and transferable to other few-shot tasks.

Empirical results are strong and reasonably broad: consistent improvements on two standard benchmarks (S3DIS, ScanNet) over four N-way/K-shot settings, with the exception noted below. The method is lightweight (a single WARM layer, distance-based prediction) relative to the complex decoders used by prior work.

The inclusion of the 'FPS + min-dist.' control is commendable and honest: it exposes that a large share of the headline gain over prior art comes from the simple distance-based head rather than from the proposed module. This is an informative finding in itself.

The supporting analyses are reasonably thorough: attention entropy/diversity metrics (Tab. 6), attention-map and segmentation visualizations (Figs. 3-4), gradient-magnitude/convergence curves (Fig. 5), and a token-count ablation (Fig. 6). The paper is clearly written and well organized.
weaknesses: The diagnosed 'distributional misalignment' is essentially a feature-scale mismatch: Tab. 2 shows D^instance of 1.14 for the prototypical tokens vs 95.06 for the support features. The authors' own ablation shows that a plain channel normalization reduces Dist(Q,K) from 288.81 to 13.30, essentially matching whitening's 13.14. The diagnostic evidence therefore does not establish that whitening (with covariance inversion) is the right remedy. The only remaining distinction between whitening and normalization is 60.16 vs 57.59 mIoU in a single setting (S3DIS S_0, 1-way 1-shot), with no variance estimate - even though the paper's own motivation shows FPS-based methods fluctuate with std ~2.4 mIoU. The claimed advantage of whitening over the much cheaper normalization is not statistically established.

The interpretation of the component ablation is questionable. In rows (b)/(c), the prototypes end up in a normalized/whitened space while the query features used in the nearest-prototype distance (Eqs. 12-13) are not, so the collapse to 14.18/10.83 mIoU is an expected consequence of a space mismatch, not evidence that alignment 'eliminates essential distributional characteristics.' Correspondingly, 'coloring' is the mathematically trivial inverse transform needed for the distance-based head to be well defined, rather than a mechanism that 'restores semantics.' A cleaner control (e.g., normalizing both prototypes and query features, or a cosine/learned classifier) is missing, and the ablation's row/column labels are inconsistent with the text (the text calls (d) 'whitening' while the table appears to mark (d) as whitening+coloring), making the central ablation hard to verify.

The paper's stated motivation is the instability of FPS-based prototypes, yet the proposed method's stability is never measured. No variance/std across episodes, seeds or initializations is reported for WARM, and the claim that attention-based generation is 'deterministic, ensuring consistent and stable performance regardless of initialization' is asserted rather than demonstrated. This is a direct gap between the stated problem and the supplied evidence, and no error bars or significance tests appear in the main tables.

There is no ablation isolating the cross-attention module itself. Obvious alternatives - a single class-mean prototype with coloring, class mean plus a learnable offset, or k-means prototypes - are never tested. Since Eq. (11) adds the class mean mu^C to every prototype and L_sim explicitly pulls prototypes toward the support features (a k-means-like objective), it is plausible that most of the benefit comes from anchoring prototypes to class statistics rather than from learned attention aggregation. The paper cannot rule this out.

Headline claim vs. control: because 'FPS + min-dist.' already reaches 51.03 (S3DIS overall) vs 43.64 for COSeg, most of the reported margin over prior art stems from the classification head/protocol rather than WARM. The abstract and introduction still advertise 'state-of-the-art performance with a significant margin' without qualifying WARM's marginal contribution (+4.63 on S3DIS, +2.20 on ScanNet over the simple baseline).

The claim in Sec. 6.2 that 'this superiority is consistently observed on the ScanNet dataset' is inaccurate: on ScanNet 1-way 1-shot, COSeg outperforms WARM on both splits (S_0: 41.73 vs 41.16; S_1: 41.82 vs 39.10).

Reproducibility and technical detail are insufficient: the feature dimension D is never stated; there is no discussion of how the covariance Sigma^C is regularized when singular or ill-conditioned (likely in 1-shot episodes with few foreground points), nor of the per-episode D x D inverse-square-root cost; it is unclear whether multi-shot prototypes are averaged before or after coloring; and no code release is mentioned. The ablation is also narrow (only S3DIS S_0, 1-way 1-shot) with no cross-dataset or cross-setting verification of the components, and the stability analysis in Tab. 1 is limited to one dataset/split/setting with a protocol ('1000 FPS initializations within an episode... accumulated among test episodes by rank') that is not fully explained.

Novelty is modest: the method is a composition of ZCA whitening (a long-standing technique) and DETR-style learnable-query cross-attention. The paper's framing overstates the depth of the 'distributional gap' problem relative to what the analysis actually shows (a scale/conditioning mismatch), and the practical takeaway - 'whiten features before attention, un-whiten after' - is largely a well-known normalization trick applied to a new task.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and underexplored issue in FS-PCS: the randomness/seed-sensitivity of FPS-based prototype construction. Table 1 provides a clean empirical demonstration of this instability (e.g., COSeg std 2.41, FPS+min_dist std 0.86 vs. WARM's zero variance), which is a useful diagnostic contribution independent of the proposed method.

The analysis of attention misalignment in Sec. 4.2 is quantitatively supported via four complementary metrics (average distance, mean distance, within-instance dispersion, anisotropy) in Table 2, showing that the distributional gap persists even after the query/key projections. This provides a principled motivation for the whitening step rather than a purely heuristic one.

The proposed WARM module is simple, deterministic, and well-motivated: ZCA-whitening aligns support features with prototypical tokens, cross-attention aggregates semantically, and coloring restores instance-specific statistics. The design choices are directly tied to the diagnosed failure modes, and the ablation (Table 5) cleanly isolates the contribution of normalization vs. whitening vs. coloring.

The plug-and-play experiments are a strong practical argument: replacing FPS prototypes with WARM improves COSeg (46.31 -> 59.26), MM-FSS (49.84 -> 52.62), and VIP-Seg (76.99 -> 78.51), demonstrating generality beyond a single framework.

Experimental evidence is broad and careful: component/loss ablations, attention entropy/diversity analysis, parametric-capacity control (Table 8, showing gain is not from added parameters since CA and WARM share the same 1.13M extra parameters), token-count ablation, and runtime/memory overhead (Table 9, showing WARM is faster than FPS due to parallelizable matrix multiplications).

Reproducibility is good: code is released, training details (optimizer, learning rate, epochs, episodes) are given, and the supplementary material provides the SVD-based reformulation and the numerical-stability derivation for regularized whitening.

The method achieves state-of-the-art results among uni-modal approaches on S3DIS with a much simpler architecture than decoder-heavy baselines, which is a non-trivial and useful finding for the community.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: whitening/coloring (ZCA) is a well-established technique (e.g., Huang et al. 2018, cited as [15]), and the core methodological contribution is its application to prototype generation in FS-PCS. The paper itself frames the contribution as "rethinking a simple architecture," which tempers the algorithmic novelty.

The S3DIS gap over the trivial 'FPS + min_dist.' baseline (51.35 -> 60.16) is large and somewhat surprising; the paper does not deeply analyze why a plain distance classifier is so strong, nor why decoder-based methods like COSeg underperform it, which would strengthen the scientific argument about prototype integrity vs. decoder capacity.

ScanNet results are less convincing: WARM is competitive among uni-modal methods but is clearly below MM-FSS (a multi-modal method). While the paper appropriately attributes this to the absence of multi-modal pretraining, this limits the claimed impact of the module to the uni-modal regime.

The entropy/diversity analysis (Table 7) is somewhat interpretive: higher entropy is argued to be better, but no independent validation links these metrics to downstream accuracy beyond the single S3DIS S0 setting, and the 'moderate but sufficient diversity' claim is qualitative.

Whitening per class in the 1-shot regime relies on covariance estimation from very few points; the regularization (Sec. 5.3, Table A1) is only ablated on S3DIS S0, and the sensitivity of the method to extremely sparse classes or to N-way K-shot settings is not thoroughly examined.

No explicit limitations section or failure-case analysis is provided; the conclusion notes the direction is underexplored but does not discuss when whitening-based alignment would fail (e.g., highly anisotropic but semantically meaningful feature directions that regularization may clip).

strengths: The paper identifies and quantitatively characterizes a real, underexplored problem in FS-PCS: the instability of FPS-based prototype construction (Tab. 1) and the distributional mismatch between learnable prototypical tokens and support features under vanilla cross-attention (Tab. 2, Fig. 1). This diagnostic analysis is well-executed and provides a concrete motivation that goes beyond anecdotal claims.

The proposed WARM module is simple, principled, and well-motivated: ZCA whitening aligns support features with the tokens before attention, and the inverse coloring step restores instance-specific statistics. The design follows directly from the measured failure modes (mean shift, dispersion, and anisotropy), making the method feel more like a reasoned solution than a hyperparameter search.

The empirical results on S3DIS are strong and clearly reported: WARM reaches 55.66 overall mIoU, outperforming the uni-modal baselines (e.g., COSeg 43.64, FPS+min-dist 51.03) and even the multi-modal MM-FSS (50.19), with a notable margin in the 1-way 1-shot setting.

The paper demonstrates genuine plug-and-play value: substituting FPS prototypes with WARM improves COSeg from 46.31 to 59.26 mIoU and MM-FSS from 49.84 to 52.62, and also improves the foreground-oversampling method VIP-Seg (Tab. A3). This generality strengthens the contribution beyond a single architecture.

Ablations are thorough and address the most likely reviewer concerns: component-wise analysis (Tab. 5), loss ablation (Tab. 6), attention entropy/diversity (Tab. 7, Fig. 4), parametric-capacity control showing gains are not merely from added parameters (Tab. 8), token-count sensitivity (Fig. 5), and runtime/memory overhead (Tab. 9). The parametric-capacity ablation in particular is a valuable control.
Reproducibility is well-supported: implementation details, optimizer settings, epoch counts, and hardware are specified, and code is stated to be publicly available.

The supplementary material adds useful depth, including the derivation of the anisotropy metric, numerical-stability handling of the whitening inverse (Eqs. 18-19), and an ablation on the eigenvalue threshold, which increases confidence in the method's robustness.
weaknesses: The central technical ingredient — whitening followed by coloring — is an established transform (closely related to the Whitening and Coloring Transform used in style transfer and to whitening-based few-shot methods). The novelty lies primarily in applying it to prototype generation in FS-PCS, which makes the contribution somewhat incremental even if effective. The paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of the relationship to prior whitening-based alignment techniques and an argument for why the FS-PCS setting requires this specific treatment.

The method section is framed entirely around a binary foreground/background formulation (C ∈ {FG, BG}), while the experiments report multi-class mIoU. It is not clearly explained how the N-way K-shot multi-class setting is handled (e.g., whether prototypes are constructed per class independently, or how background is treated across N classes). This gap complicates understanding of how the method generalizes beyond 1-way 1-shot and should be clarified.

The state-of-the-art claim is dataset-dependent: on ScanNet the method is competitive rather than superior, and it underperforms MM-FSS and occasionally FPS+min-dist in several settings (e.g., 1-way 1-shot S1: 39.10 vs 43.37; overall 41.21 vs 44.53). The paper acknowledges this, but the headline framing would be more balanced if the limitations on ScanNet were discussed in the abstract/conclusion.

The alignment claim is somewhat implicit. Whitening removes the covariance structure of the support features, but the paper does not directly verify that the whitened distribution actually matches the distribution of the prototypical tokens (which are learnable and could drift). The anisotropy values reported for the tokens are small (5.36), consistent with the assumption, but a more direct alignment measure (e.g., a distributional distance after whitening) would strengthen the central argument.

The interpretation of the attention statistics is somewhat ambiguous: WARM produces higher entropy (0.8387 vs 0.2079), which the authors read as semantic breadth, but higher entropy could also reflect less discriminative attention. The diversity metric partially addresses this, and qualitative results (Fig. 4) support the claim, yet the argument remains partly qualitative and could be reinforced with a quantitative link between attention entropy and segmentation accuracy.

The number of prototypical tokens is large (100 per class, 200 total in the 1-way setting). While the token-count ablation shows stability for M ≥ 50 on S3DIS, the sensitivity on ScanNet at M = 10 and the choice of 100 tokens deserve more justification, particularly regarding the learnable-parameter budget relative to the support set size.

The improvement of WARM over COSeg when used as a drop-in replacement is very large (46.31 → 59.26). While plausible given the reported FPS instability, such a large gain warrants a deeper analysis (e.g., interaction with COSeg's decoder) to rule out any protocol or tuning asymmetry favoring the replacement.

The 1-way 1-shot setting dominates the analysis, and the strongest gains appear there; gains in 2-way settings are smaller and, in some cases, WARM is only comparable to simpler baselines. A more focused discussion of where and why the advantage diminishes would improve the scientific clarity.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies and quantifies a real problem in FS-PCS: FPS-based prototype construction is stochastic and unstable (Tab. 1 shows large min/max spread and negative margins for COSeg), and it provides a distributional analysis (Tab. 2) showing a sizable gap in mean, dispersion, and anisotropy between learnable prototypical tokens and support features.

The proposed fix (ZCA whitening before cross-attention, coloring/inverse-whitening after) is simple, principled, symmetric, and easy to implement, and the regularized whitening (Eq. 12 / supplement B) sensibly addresses ill-conditioning and noise amplification for sparse point sets.

Empirical results are strong on the primary benchmark: S3DIS overall mIoU 55.66 with a large margin in the 1-way 1-shot setting (60.16 vs. 46.31 for COSeg and 51.35 for FPS+min-dist), and the plug-and-play experiments (COSeg 46.31→59.26, MM-FSS 49.84→52.62, VIP-Seg 76.99→78.51) demonstrate genuine versatility.

The ablation suite is unusually thorough: component-wise alignment (Tab. 5), loss terms (Tab. 6), attention entropy/diversity (Tab. 7), parametric-capacity control (Tab. 8), token count (Fig. 5), and runtime/memory (Tab. 9), the last showing a clear practical advantage over sequential FPS.

The paper is generally well written and honest about scope, acknowledging that ScanNet gains are competitive rather than SOTA and that the contribution targets prototype construction rather than feature quality or decoder design.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The whitening–coloring (WCT) transform is a long-standing, well-known technique (e.g., style transfer, AdaIN-style statistics alignment); the contribution is essentially its application to cross-attention prototype generation in FS-PCS, so the core technical mechanism is not new and the architectural change is small.

The central claim that whitening yields 'semantic' rather than spatial attention is supported mainly by entropy/diversity statistics and t-SNE visualizations (Fig. 1a, Fig. 4, Tab. 7). The causal link between decorrelation and semantic grouping is asserted rather than rigorously established, and the metrics are indirect proxies.

Some ablations have a confounded interpretation: whitening alone (Tab. 5c, 10.83 mIoU) and normalization alone (14.18) collapse largely because prototypes are then compared to query features living in a different (un-restored) space, which makes the near-catastrophic drops less informative about the mechanism than the text implies.

The headline 'state-of-the-art' is confined to S3DIS; on ScanNet the method is only competitive among uni-modal approaches and trails the multi-modal MM-FSS, and the paper does not fully disentangle how much of the gain stems from the 200 learnable tokens versus the whitening/coloring operation.
The threshold schedule in Eq. (12) is heuristic and its motivation (noise upper bound) is only loosely justified; the supplement mitigates this but the main text presents it as settled.

Presentation issues: a blank code URL despite claiming public availability, minor notation/typo problems (e.g., 'Dispersion'), and dense figure/table layouts that make the alignment arguments harder to follow than necessary.
